What Optimization Services Does

Automated analytics, applied by engineers who know buildings.

Why it belongs in the service

A control sequence corrected inside an air handler is an engineering result. Whether the campus is spending less energy this year than last is a business result. Optimization has to produce both, and they are measured in different places.

Atrius is where the second question gets answered, and where Navitas verifies that improvements made inside the building actually show up on the bill.

Questions Leadership Can Finally Ask

Normalized data turns a stack of bills into a set of answers.

Which facilities use the most energy?
Ranked by intensity rather than raw consumption, so size is not mistaken for inefficiency.
Which facilities changed this year?
Year over year movement per building, weather normalized, with the outliers surfaced first.
Where did baseload increase?
Overnight and unoccupied consumption, which is where equipment left running tends to show up.
Did the optimization work reduce consumption?
Pre and post comparison against a normalized baseline, not a before and after guess.
Is the campus performing better than last year?
Campus level rollups that leadership and finance can use without a facility background.
What should we budget next year?
Consumption and cost trajectory by account, so utility budgets are built on trend rather than on last year plus a percentage.

Two Views, One Service

Building level intelligence. Portfolio level intelligence. Engineering judgment in the middle.

Neither view is sufficient on its own. One tells you what a machine is doing wrong on a Tuesday afternoon. The other tells you what a year of those Tuesdays cost the organization.

Why Healthcare

In a hospital, how the mechanical systems run is an operations issue before it is an energy issue.

Optimization in healthcare is not simply about lowering a utility bill. The same corrections that reduce consumption usually make the building more stable, more comfortable and less likely to interrupt clinical operations.

What improves alongside the energy number

Patient and staff comfort
Critical environment stability
Indoor air quality
Equipment reliability
Fewer emergency calls
Central plant performance
Capital planning
Sustainability reporting
Budget predictability

Air handlers serving operating rooms, imaging suites and patient floors do not get to fail quietly. Optimization work is scheduled, coordinated and documented around that reality.

From Reactive To Proactive

Both are loops. Only one of them improves the building.

Most facility organizations are excellent at responding. The limitation is that responding starts when somebody notices, and a great deal of waste never generates a complaint.

Today

Traditional Facility Operations

1A complaint comes in. A room is too warm, too cold, too loud.
2An operator leaves what they were doing and investigates.
3The immediate problem is corrected, often with an override.
4The system keeps operating, override still in place.
5Another complaint appears somewhere else.
Repeats, without getting better
With Optimization Services

Continuous Optimization

1Analytics identify abnormal operation, usually before anyone complains.
2A Navitas engineer reviews the condition and the evidence behind it.
3The opportunity is prioritized against cost, comfort and risk.
4The correction is implemented with staff and contractors.
5Performance is verified against the data, not assumed.
6The system stays monitored, so drift is caught the next time.
Repeats, and compounds

One Finding, End To End

A cooling valve failed on a Tuesday. The building hid it for four days.

The detection shown here is a real SkySpark capture. What the building did next is the reason a service like this exists. The response dates are illustrative; the pattern is not.

Tuesday morning · Detection

A chilled water valve fails at the air handler

Discharge air temperature on AHU-1 falls from the low seventies to 47 degrees and stays there. Nothing goes into alarm. The unit is running, the fan is running, and as far as the sequence is concerned it is doing its job.

SkySpark
The same morning · What the building did

Seventeen terminal boxes go to reheat, and the rooms stay comfortable

Every VAV box on the unit is now receiving air far colder than it asked for, and every one of them does exactly what it was designed to do: it calls for heat to protect its space. Classrooms, labs, offices, all of them, every occupied hour, for four days.

The building, doing what it was told
Why nobody called it in

There was no complaint to respond to

This is the part that matters. Reheat held the spaces at temperature, so nobody was uncomfortable, no work order was written and no operator was paged. A traditional response cycle starts when somebody notices. Here there was nothing to notice.

The gap this service closes
Days 1 to 3 · Engineering review

An engineer opens the values and confirms it

Discharge air at 47.05 degrees on Tuesday morning, with the heat stage state of every box on the unit beside it. That is enough to separate a failed valve from a reheat sequence behaving as designed, and enough to say what has to be touched to fix it.

Navitas engineering
Implementation

The valve is corrected with your team, not around them

Repair or replacement coordinated with facility staff and the controls contractor, scheduled around the spaces the unit serves. In a hospital that scheduling constraint is the hard part, and it is planned rather than improvised.

Facility staff · Controls partner
Afterward · Verification and confirmation

The analytics confirm it held, and the utility data shows what it was worth

Discharge air tracks setpoint again and the reheat calls fall back to what the schedule actually requires. The finding clears. If it returns, it is caught the same week rather than the same year, and Atrius shows whether the correction moved building consumption against a weather normalized baseline.

Nobody called. That is the whole problem, and it is the part analytics are actually good at.

Now multiply it

One air handler, one valve, four days. A healthcare campus runs dozens of air handlers, two central plants and thousands of points, continuously, through every season and every schedule change. The question is not whether conditions like this exist right now. It is whether anything is looking.

The Human Element

Analytics find signals.
Engineers turn them into action.

Software can tell you that a valve and a sensor disagree. It cannot tell you that the air handler serves a pre-op area, that the unit is scheduled for replacement in two years, that the controls contractor is already on site next week, or that the real fix is a sequence written badly at commissioning.

That judgment is the service. Navitas engineers and facility professionals sit between the analytics and your building, and they stay involved after the recommendation is made.

This is not a software subscription. It is an engineering relationship that happens to be extremely well instrumented.

Interpret the findings
Separate the conditions that matter from the ones that are the sequence working as designed.
Understand operational priorities
Critical spaces, clinical schedules, staffing and what your team can realistically take on this quarter.
Identify practical solutions
A setpoint change, a rewritten sequence, a repair, or a capital recommendation when that is the honest answer.
Verify the result
Confirm the change held in the data, and reopen it when it does not.
Report it in the right language
Engineering detail for the plant. Cost, risk and trend for the executive team.
